evals.prompt: I'm head of platform at Veltrix, a B2B inventory-management SaaS with about 400 customers. Our CEO came back from a conference convinced we need to ship an MCP server this quarter so we're 'AI-native', and he's floated charging AI agents per API call as a new revenue line. Current state: a REST API that covers maybe 60% of product functionality, an OpenAPI file someone wrote a year ago that no longer matches the live API, and no webhooks. Our logs show zero agent traffic and no customer has ever asked about MCP. I have two backend engineers. Draft our integration-surface plan for the next two quarters.
evals.expected_output: A sequenced surface plan that parks MCP for lack of agent-demand signals, fixes the drifting spec and shallow REST coverage first, schedules webhooks on the same foundation, labels per-call agent monetization speculative, and matches concurrency to the two-engineer capacity.
expectations: Recommends against building the MCP server this quarter, parking it until agent-demand signals (RFPs requiring MCP compatibility, or observed agent traffic) appear
Names the absence of agent signals (zero agent traffic, no customer asks) as the reason MCP is parked, rather than arguing only from team effort or generic prioritization
Identifies fixing the drifting OpenAPI spec as a prerequisite scheduled before any derived surface (SDKs, MCP, generated docs) enters the plan
States that when MCP is eventually built it must be derived or generated from the existing API contract, never hand-built as a separate product
Flags the 60% API coverage as a shallow-API-first failure: partners discover mid-integration that later steps still need manual touches, so depth is probed per capability
Sequences REST completion plus webhooks as the first surfaces, noting webhooks ride the same infrastructure rather than opening a new paradigm
Labels the per-call agent monetization idea speculative, noting unproven unit economics and that observed per-call volumes are tiny and partly wash-traded
Caps concurrent new-surface builds at the stated two-engineer capacity, sequencing surfaces one at a time
Includes review triggers that reopen the plan early, among them agent-demand signals moving from none to present
Justifies delaying higher-abstraction surfaces via the dependency mechanism (Hyrum's Law or equivalent: once enough consumers depend on observable behavior, the contract is near-impossible to change)
Establishes the buyer type (developer-chosen vs non-technical buyer) via a question or an explicit audience map before or while ranking surfaces
Each scheduled surface carries a named audience and the demand signal justifying it, plus a reversal-cost tier and an owner

evals.prompt: I run platform engineering at Corvana, a logistics SaaS. Our new mobile team lead insists we replace our public REST API with GraphQL - he says REST is legacy, every modern platform is moving to GraphQL, and our own mobile app genuinely over-fetches on the shipment-list screen. External integrators haven't complained about anything. We have 6 platform engineers, no internal GraphQL experience, and a stable OpenAPI-driven REST API with webhooks already live. Should GraphQL be next on our surface roadmap, and what would committing to it actually mean?
evals.expected_output: A recommendation declining a public GraphQL surface now because the pain is first-party rather than integrator-confirmed, carrying the overhead and reversal-cost figures, the Shopify precedent in both directions, and the condition that would promote GraphQL later.
expectations: Declines to schedule a public GraphQL surface now because the over-fetching pain is first-party mobile, not confirmed by external integrators
States that GraphQL is promoted only on named, integrator-confirmed pain (client-driven data access, over/under-fetching, N+1), never as a default REST replacement
Carries the roughly 20-40% initial-build overhead plus N+1 and authorization complexity as GraphQL's standing cost
Classifies a public GraphQL schema as a high reversal-cost, tight and binding contract, in contrast with additive REST changes being cheap to unwind
Rebuts the 'REST is legacy' claim with REST's dominant adoption (on the order of 93% vs 33% for GraphQL, or equivalent framing of REST as the near-universal substrate)
Cites Shopify's GraphQL-first Admin API in both directions: evidence a major platform anchored on it, and evidence of significant developer pushback over verbosity
Notes that surfaces persist for different consumers rather than replacing one another, so GraphQL would not retire the REST contract integrators depend on
Notes the team's lack of internal GraphQL experience as raising the option's cost (a team already running GraphQL internally gets it cheaper)
Frames the paradigm switch as a long-horizon (about two-year) commitment rather than a quarter project
Names the condition that would promote GraphQL anyway: external integrators confirming the data-access pain
Keeps the stable spec-driven REST-plus-webhooks foundation as the base later surfaces derive from

evals.prompt: I'm VP product at Tandemly, HR-compliance software sold to office managers and HR directors - none of them write code. Sales says deals close when we demo turnkey integrations with payroll tools, and prospects expect setup within an afternoon. Meanwhile our board keeps quoting 'every company should be API-first' and wants a public REST API on the roadmap before anything else. We have no public API today, one platform engineer, plus some contractor budget. What should our integration surface order be?
evals.expected_output: A layered plan that leads with the embedded/turnkey surface for the non-technical buyer while still building the API foundation underneath, justified by buyer-type mapping, with candidate sequences, capacity-matched sequencing, and demand signals recorded per surface.
expectations: Leads the sequence with the embedded/turnkey layer, justified by the non-technical buyer and the hours-level time-to-value requirement
Maps the buyer type explicitly (who chooses the product) before ranking surfaces, rather than jumping to a build order
Treats API-first and embedded as layers rather than rivals, refusing both the board's blanket API-first framing and an embedded-only answer
Plans the API foundation underneath the embedded layer, naming that retrofitting an API onto a UI-first product later is the expensive direction

Uses the contrast between a developer-sold API platform and a business-owner-sold checkout button (Stripe vs PayPal or equivalent) as evidence the same industry supports opposite surface orders by buyer
Warns that a surface reaching only the economic buyer or only the technical user stalls the deal
Sequences one surface at a time matched to the one-engineer capacity
Schedules no SDKs or MCP before a stable API contract exists
Cites the retention/switching-cost argument for the API foundation: an API embedded in customer production code costs engineering hours to leave, not a cancellation click
Presents 2-3 candidate sequences with trade-offs and a recommendation for the user to pick or blend, rather than one dictated plan
Records the demand signal for the embedded surface (sales naming turnkey integrations as deal-closers) instead of scheduling it on taste

evals.prompt: Platform PM at Quorrel, a developer-facing observability tool. Three signals are pulling different ways: (1) our community Discord and GitHub have loudly asked for a Terraform provider and a CLI for months - 400+ reactions on the issue; (2) sales says two enterprise renewals stalled last quarter because we can't export telemetry to the customer's warehouse; (3) API logs show 61% of REST traffic carries our Python library's user-agent. Leadership wants to pick by 'what the community wants' since community is our brand. What do we build first?
evals.expected_output: A prioritization that puts the warehouse/bulk export first on the strength of the stalled renewals, ranks telemetry second and community asks third with reasons, applies the helper-library precedent to the 61% figure, and routes the bulk surface by demand shape.
expectations: Ranks the stalled enterprise renewals as the highest-weight signal and schedules the warehouse/bulk export surface first
States the weighting rationale: pipeline blockers are low-frequency but high-severity, and a named blocked deal outranks any volume metric
Ranks the 61% library user-agent share as the strongest volume signal, second behind the deal blockers
Interprets the 61% figure through the documented helper-library precedent (roughly 77% of a major platform's REST traffic via library user-agents justifying SDK formalization and generation)
Ranks community asks (Discord and GitHub reactions) third, as real but cheap to emit and easy to over-weight
Pushes back on leadership's pick-by-community framing instead of adopting it
Parks or defers the community-requested CLI and Terraform provider until confirmed against the higher-weight signals
Distinguishes which downstream design owns the bulk surface by demand shape: file/lake export versus rows synced through an ELT tool
Records the audience and the justifying demand signal for every scheduled or deferred surface
Sets a review cadence or trigger tied to the deal-blocker log and telemetry changes reopening the plan

evals.prompt: CTO at Mirelet, an 11-person fintech-infrastructure startup. We just raised and want to go big on platform: this quarter we plan to simultaneously launch webhooks, official SDKs in Python, Node, Go, Java and Ruby, a GraphQL endpoint, and an embeddable dashboard widget. Our REST API works fine, though the OpenAPI file lives in a wiki page and gets updated by hand when someone remembers. We also have no usage analytics on the API yet - we figured we'd add those after the new surfaces are live. Roadmap review is Friday. Sanity-check the plan?
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the simultaneous launch that sequences one surface at a time within a stated capacity, blocks SDK generation on a CI-linted spec, fixes the drifting wiki spec first, drops GraphQL absent integrator pain, and moves telemetry instrumentation to the front.
expectations: Rejects the simultaneous multi-surface launch and sequences one new surface at a time within a stated capacity number
States the reason: several concurrent launches yield half-measured surfaces with no clean signal from any, plus a standing maintenance bill for all
Asks for or forces a sustained-capacity number: how many surfaces the team can build, document, support, and keep releasing for years
Blocks the five-language SDK plan until the spec is a linted source of truth in CI, because SDKs derive from that contract
Flags the hand-updated wiki OpenAPI file as spec drift to fix before any derived surface is scheduled
Cites the one-spec-propagates-everywhere pattern (major platforms generating SDKs, docs, and MCP from one OpenAPI source of truth)
Defers or removes the GraphQL endpoint absent a named, integrator-confirmed pain
Moves per-client and per-surface usage telemetry instrumentation to an early plan item instead of after launch
Keeps webhooks as the near-term addition riding the existing REST infrastructure
Cites the capacity-matched precedent: SDK languages added only once tooling made supporting them sustainable, or the principle that two surfaces done properly beat six done badly
Assigns surviving surfaces reversal-cost tiers, including server SDKs as high because method signatures bake directly into customer code

evals.prompt: Head of product platform at Nuvaris, a B2B spend-management SaaS. Sales lost two enterprise deals to a competitor because the prospects wanted our transaction data available in Snowflake, and customer success reports AI assistants increasingly making calls against our API. We already run solid REST plus webhooks and generated SDKs off a clean OpenAPI spec. Four platform engineers. I want next year's surface roadmap covering warehouse sharing, a CLI, and 'agent access'. For the CLI, my staff engineer already drafted a spec with pretty ANSI table output. Lay out the plan per surface.
evals.expected_output: A per-surface roadmap that schedules warehouse sharing on the lost deals, redesigns the CLI for dual human-and-agent audiences, schedules a derived MCP layer on the observed agent traffic, carries all five handoff fields per surface, and sets a review cadence with reopen triggers.
expectations: Schedules the warehouse/bulk sharing surface on the strength of the two lost deals, treating the pipeline blocker as the highest-weight signal
Revises the CLI spec to serve dual audiences: readable table output for humans plus JSON with clean stdout/stderr separation for agents
Notes the CLI has no dedicated downstream design owner, so its design decisions are recorded in the plan itself
Schedules the agent-access surface (MCP) because observed agent traffic is a real demand signal, distinguishing this from hype-driven scheduling
Positions MCP as a thin layer derived or generated from the existing stable contract, sequenced after the foundation and never hand-built
Keeps concurrent new-surface builds within the four-engineer capacity, sequencing the three surfaces rather than launching all at once
Every surface entry carries all five handoff fields: target audience, justifying demand signal, reversal-cost tier, capacity owner, and the owning downstream design or an inline decision
Separates this plan's job (whether and when each surface ships) from per-surface design (how), which is handed off
Sets a review date (quarterly or similar) plus named reopen triggers such as a new deal blocker or agent-signal changes
Maps each surface to a distinct consumer class (BI consumers for warehouse sharing, humans and agents for the CLI, agent clients for MCP) rather than one ladder every consumer climbs
Records what evidence the next review must re-check rather than re-arguing the whole plan
